unit.title: Perform basic welding using oxyacetylene welding process (OAW) - Fuel Gas Welding

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A drawing calls for a gas-welded butt joint in 6 mm mild steel plate. Which method and edge preparation are usually best?
options: Rightward, with a 60° single-V preparation
Leftward, with square edges and no gap
Leftward, with flanged edges melted down
Rightward, with square edges butted tight together

questions.stem: On thick plate, why does rightward welding usually use less gas and filler rod than leftward welding?
options: The rod is melted by the outer flame only
The flame is set carburising, which saves oxygen
The V is narrower, so less metal fills it
The joint is made in one thin run with no root

questions.stem: Which set of details belongs in a welding procedure (WPS) for an oxy-acetylene butt weld?
options: Welder's name, pay rate and hours worked
Nozzle size, pressures, flame and filler
Customer's address and the job's price
Gas supplier and the delivery dates

questions.stem: A trainee's test weld looks good, but he used a bigger nozzle than the WPS gives. As team leader, what is the right decision?
options: Accept it, as the weld looks good
Accept it, and note the nozzle on the job card
Change the WPS to the bigger nozzle for everyone
Have it re-welded as the WPS says

questions.stem: A nozzle uses about 300 litres of acetylene an hour. A job needs 5 hours of welding. About how much acetylene will be used?
options: 600 litres
1 000 litres
1 500 litres
3 000 litres

questions.stem: A job uses 2 000 litres of oxygen at J$2 a litre and 1 800 litres of acetylene at J$5 a litre. What is the total gas cost?
Your team will gas weld a cracked trailer frame at a customer's yard in May Pen. Which check matters most before the torch is lit?
options: That the trailer is parked in full sun
That the tyres are at the right pressure
That the customer has the trailer's papers
What is behind the weld that could burn

questions.stem: One acetylene cylinder cannot give enough flow for a large heating nozzle. What is the usual safe answer?
options: Open the cylinder valve fully for more flow
Couple two or more cylinders to share the draw
Lay the cylinder on its side so more comes out
Raise the working pressure above the limit

questions.stem: Why do makers set a low upper limit on the working pressure of acetylene?
options: Free acetylene can break down and explode
It soaks into the hose and makes it brittle
The flame becomes too cold to weld steel
The working gauge cannot read that high

questions.stem: Why is a two-stage regulator often chosen for long welding jobs?
options: Oxygen and acetylene can share one regulator
No flashback arrestors are then needed
The pressure stays steady as the cylinder empties
It doubles the gas held in the cylinder

questions.stem: What is special about an injector (low-pressure) torch, compared with an equal-pressure torch?
options: It works with oxygen only, and no fuel gas
Its oxygen jet draws the fuel gas through
It cannot be fitted with flashback arrestors
It can only be used for cutting, not welding

questions.stem: A flashback arrestor has a flame-stop element and a non-return valve. What does the flame-stop element do?
options: Stops gas flowing back up the hose
Lowers the pressure from the cylinder
Filters dirt out of the gas
Puts out a flame trying to pass through

questions.stem: A regulator has oil on its inlet thread. What should the team leader do?
options: Wipe it with a rag and fit it as normal
Fit it on the acetylene side only
Take it out of use and send it for service
Blow oxygen through it to clear the oil

questions.stem: With the torch valves shut, you close the oxygen cylinder valve for a few minutes. The oxygen high-pressure gauge slowly falls. What does this show?
options: A leak somewhere on the oxygen side
The regulator diaphragm needs oiling
The oxygen cylinder was overfilled
The working pressure is set too low

questions.stem: A damaged hose has been cut and joined with a short pipe and two screw-type hose clips. What should be done?
options: Wrap tape over the clips and keep using it as normal
Use it on the oxygen side only
Keep it, as long as it passes a leak test
Replace it, or repair it with proper fittings

questions.stem: Burning acetylene fully needs about 2½ times its volume of oxygen, yet a neutral flame takes about equal volumes from the torch. Where does the rest of the oxygen come from?
options: From oxygen held inside the acetylene
From the air around the outer flame
From the oxide on the steel surface
From the regulator, which adds extra

questions.stem: A worn part is to be hardfaced with a hard-wearing rod. Which flame is normally used?
options: A carburising flame
A neutral flame
An oxidising flame
A cutting flame with the lever pressed

questions.stem: During a long weld, a trainee's neutral flame slowly turns oxidising without him touching the valves. What is the most likely cause?
options: The oxygen hose is too long
The filler rod is too thick
The acetylene supply is falling off
The plate has been cleaned too well

questions.stem: In rightward welding, how are the torch and filler rod moved?
options: Torch weaves side to side; rod stays still in the pool
Torch moves steadily along; rod makes small loops
Rod goes ahead of the flame and the torch weaves
Both are held still and lifted in and out together

questions.stem: In rightward welding, the flame points back over the weld just made. What is one benefit of this?
options: It cleans rust off the plate ahead of the weld
It melts the filler rod before it reaches the pool
It allows an oxidising flame to be used safely
It shields the hot weld and slows its cooling

questions.stem: What happens if the filler rod is far too thick for the thin sheet being welded?
options: It melts too quickly and drips off
It turns the flame oxidising
It chills the pool and gives poor fusion
It adds too much copper to the weld

questions.stem: A vertical butt joint in 3 mm steel sheet is to be gas welded. Which way is it usually welded, and why?
options: Upward, so the pool sits on the weld below
Downward, so gravity pulls metal into the root
Downward, very fast, so the pool cannot sag
Sideways, after turning the job on its edge

questions.stem: When gas welding overhead, what matters most to stop molten metal falling?
options: A large nozzle and a hot, slow weld
A long flame held well away from the plate
A thick rod pushed hard into the pool
A small pool, kept well under control

questions.stem: A small-bore steel pipe joint is gas welded with the pipe fixed horizontal, so it cannot be turned. How is the weld usually made?
options: In one pass, from the top down both sides
In two halves, each from the bottom up over the top
On the top half only, as the bottom is hidden from view
From the top down, as fast as possible

questions.stem: Why are the tacks on a pipe butt joint spaced evenly round it, for example three or four tacks?
options: To hold the gap and line-up even all round
So the full joint need not be welded
So the pipe can be turned with tongs
To let gas inside the pipe escape

questions.stem: Why is a cast iron part preheated, and then cooled slowly, when it is gas welded?
options: To burn the flux off before welding starts
So the filler rod melts at a lower heat
To stop it cracking as it heats and cools
To make the iron soft enough to bend

questions.stem: What makes gas welding aluminium hard for a welder used to steel?
options: It melts at a much higher heat than steel
It shows no colour change before it melts
It cannot be welded with any flux at all
It needs an oxidising flame to melt

questions.stem: After gas welding aluminium with flux, why must every bit of flux be washed off?
options: It makes the weld too hard to file
It spoils the colour of the paint
It is saved and used again next time
Left on, it takes up damp and corrodes

questions.stem: A customer wants a galvanised (zinc-coated) steel bracket gas welded. What should be done first?
options: Weld over the zinc, as it protects the weld
Burn the zinc off quickly with an oxidising flame
Remove the zinc near the joint and use extraction
Weld it in a closed room so fumes stay inside

questions.stem: Two 1.5 m lengths of 2 mm sheet are to be butt welded. Which plan best controls distortion?
options: Tack closely, then weld in short back-step lengths
Tack only the two ends, then weld straight through
Weld one end fully, then tack the other end
Weld from both ends at once to meet in the middle

questions.stem: For a long butt seam in sheet, the gap is sometimes set wider at the far end than at the start. Why?
options: To use up more of the filler rod
To make the weld wider at the end
So the plates can be lined up again later
The gap closes up as the weld moves along

questions.stem: Before a single-V butt weld in 6 mm plate, the two plates are tacked at a slight upward angle (preset). Why?
options: To give a better view of the root
So they pull flat as the weld shrinks
So less filler rod is needed
So the flame cannot reach the root

questions.stem: In a guided bend test on a butt weld, which part of the weld does a root bend stretch?
options: The root side, underneath the weld
The face (cap) of the weld
The parent metal far from the weld
Only the tack welds at each end

questions.stem: A bend test strip splits open along one edge of the weld, showing a smooth face where weld and plate never joined. Which fault does this show?
options: Porosity
Undercut
Lack of side fusion
Excess penetration

questions.stem: A specification limits how far the penetration bead may stick out under a pipe butt weld. Why is too much penetration a fault?
options: It makes the joint far too strong
It narrows the bore and raises stress there
It means too little filler rod was used in the joint
It shows the nozzle was too small

questions.stem: In a nick-break test, the weld is notched with a saw and broken open. What is the test for?
options: To measure how hard the weld face is
To check the weld's size with a gauge
To see how well paint sticks to the weld face
To look inside it for holes and poor fusion

questions.stem: A test piece is cut across a weld, smoothed and etched with a mild acid (a macro test). What can the inspector see?
options: The chemical make-up of the rod
The gas pressures that were used
The weld's shape, fusion and penetration
The welder's name and the date

questions.stem: One trainee's gas welds keep showing gas holes, though the rod and plate are clean. Which is the most likely cause?
options: He lifts the flame away, leaving the pool bare
His nozzle is one size too small for the plate
He places too many tacks on each joint
He uses copper-coated filler rod

questions.stem: Undercut is found along the edges of a vertical gas weld. What is the most likely cause?
options: Too much filler rod added in the centre of the weld
A carburising flame on clean plate
No tacks were placed before welding
Too much heat and too little filler at the edges

questions.stem: You see a trainee open both torch valves wide and then light the torch with a loud bang. What should you do?
options: Let him carry on, as the flame did light
Stop him and show the right lighting order again
Turn up the oxygen so the torch lights more easily
Tell him to light it with a match next time

questions.stem: A trainee hangs his lit torch on the cylinder trolley while he fetches more rod. What is the main danger?
options: The flame can heat a cylinder or burn a hose
The nozzle will cool down and then block up fully
Some gas will be wasted
The filler rod will rust

questions.stem: After a flashback, the outside of an acetylene cylinder is getting hot. What should be done?
options: Carry it outside at once and lay it down on the grass
Open its valve fully so all the gas escapes quickly
Shut the valve if safe, clear the area, call fire service
Keep welding, as the heat will soon go away by itself

questions.stem: Why is extra ventilation needed for gas welding inside a small room, even on clean mild steel?
options: Acetylene smoke makes all the welds full of gas holes
The flame gives off harmful gases and uses up air
The heat makes the gauges read wrongly
Clean steel gives off zinc fumes

questions.stem: A trainee gets a small burn from a spark. After first aid, what should the team leader do?
options: Nothing more, as the burn is small
Tell the trainee to keep it quiet
Wait to see if it happens again
Record it and find out what caused it

questions.stem: Why should a team leader keep a weld record (who welded each joint, the settings and test results) for a job?
options: So welders can be paid by the weld
So the job needs no more inspection
So the work can be traced if a problem shows up
So the customer can choose the next gas supplier

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A nozzle chart gives an acetylene pressure of 7 psi. Using 1 bar = 14.5 psi, what is this in bar, to one decimal place?
Oxygen costs J$3 a litre. How much does 1 500 litres cost, in J$?
What do the letters HAZ stand for, when talking about the metal beside a weld?
Which simple destructive test breaks a fillet weld open so that its root fusion can be seen?
What is the name for a set of gas cylinders joined together to feed one supply line?
A butt weld 1.2 m long is welded at 80 mm per minute. How many minutes does it take?
What are the copper or steel bars called that are clamped beside a thin-sheet seam to draw heat away?
What is the part of the torch called where the oxygen and acetylene meet and mix?
When acetylene burns fully in the outer flame, water vapour and which other gas are given off?
Each metre of weld uses 0.25 kg of filler rod. How many kg are needed for 18 m of weld?
On a welding symbol, what type of weld does a triangle on the reference line call for?
On a welding symbol, what does a small flag where the arrow meets the reference line mean?
What is the test position code for a plate butt weld in the vertical position?
What is the test position code for a pipe butt weld with the pipe fixed horizontal, so it cannot be turned?
What is the name of the flat, unbevelled strip left along the bottom edge of a V preparation?

essays.stem: You lead a team that must gas weld 20 small brackets in 3 mm mild steel sheet for a customer in Mandeville. Explain how you would plan the job: the procedure, the equipment and gas, the people and the checks.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would read the drawing and the order: the metal, its thickness, the joints, the sizes and the number needed. I would write or check a simple WPS: leftward method, the nozzle size and gas pressures from the maker's chart, a neutral flame, the filler rod size, the tack spacing and the welding order. I would work out how much gas and rod the job needs, check the cylinders have enough, and order more if not. I would make a jig so every bracket is the same. Before work starts I would check each gas set: arrestors fitted, hoses sound, no leaks, cylinders chained upright. I would give each team member a task and brief them on the WPS and the safety rules. The first bracket is checked fully against the drawing before the rest are made. During the job I would check the welds and sizes, and at the end I would record the checks, the gas used and any problems in a short report.
markingPoints: Reads the drawing and order, and writes or checks a WPS (method, nozzle, pressures, flame, rod)
Works out and checks gas and rod needed
Checks the equipment safely before work (arrestors, hoses, leaks, cylinders secured)
Briefs and gives tasks to the team; uses a jig for repeat work
First-off check, checks during the job, and a record or report at the end

essays.stem: Compare leftward and rightward gas welding. Say which you would choose for 2 mm sheet and for 8 mm plate, and explain why.
essays.modelAnswer: In leftward welding (for a right-handed welder) the weld moves from right to left. The rod is held in front of the flame and dipped into the front of the pool, and the torch is weaved a little. The flame spreads over the cold plate ahead, which helps on thin metal but makes it hard to control a large pool. In rightward welding the weld moves from left to right. The flame points back at the finished weld and the rod follows behind, making small loops, while the torch moves steadily along. The welder can see the root better, the V can be narrower (about 60° instead of about 80°), and less gas and rod are used, so it is faster on thick plate and the weld cools more slowly. For 2 mm sheet I would choose leftward, because it gives better control of a small pool and less risk of burning through. For 8 mm plate I would choose rightward, because it gives better root fusion with less filler, gas and distortion.
markingPoints: Describes leftward: direction, rod ahead of flame, torch weave
Describes rightward: direction, flame back over weld, rod loops, steady torch
Rightward benefits on thick plate: narrower V, less gas and rod, better view and fusion
Chooses leftward for 2 mm sheet with a reason
Chooses rightward for 8 mm plate with a reason

essays.stem: List the main details that a WPS for oxy-acetylene butt welding of 6 mm mild steel plate should give, and explain how you would check that a welder works to it.
essays.modelAnswer: The WPS should give: the process (oxy-acetylene welding); the parent metal and the thickness range it covers; the joint type and edge preparation, such as a single V of about 60° with the root face and root gap; the welding position; the method (rightward for this thickness); the nozzle size and the oxygen and acetylene pressures from the maker's chart; the flame type (neutral); the filler rod type and diameter; the number of runs and the cleaning between them; any preheat; and the inspection and tests needed. To check the welder works to it, I would first make sure the welder has passed a test on this procedure. Before welding I would check the fit-up, gap and nozzle size, and watch the flame being set. During welding I would watch the method and the speed, and afterwards I would inspect the weld and compare it with the WPS. Anything outside the WPS is stopped and recorded, and the work is redone or the WPS is reviewed by the supervisor.
markingPoints: Process, metal and thickness, joint design and position
Method, nozzle size, gas pressures and flame type
Filler rod, runs, preheat and the inspection required
Checks the welder is qualified, and checks fit-up and settings before welding
Watches during welding, inspects after, and stops and records work outside the WPS

essays.stem: Before production starts, sample gas-welded butt joints are made. Explain how you would inspect and test them, including visual checks and at least two destructive tests.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first do a visual inspection in good light, with a magnifier and a weld gauge. On the face I would look for an even width and height, smooth ripples, no undercut, no cracks, no surface holes and a filled crater. Underneath I would look for even penetration along the full length, not too little and not too much. I would check the plates are in line and not badly distorted. Then I would cut test strips across the weld. In a bend test, strips are bent round a former, some with the face stretched and some with the root stretched. A sound weld bends without opening up; cracks or splits show poor fusion or holes. In a nick-break test the weld is notched with a saw and broken, so the broken face can be checked for gas holes and unfused areas. A macro test, where a cut face is smoothed and etched, shows the weld shape and penetration. I would record all results and compare them with the specification before allowing production to start.
markingPoints: Visual checks on the face: size, ripples, undercut, cracks, holes, crater
Visual checks on the root: even penetration, alignment and distortion
Bend test (face and root) described, with what a pass and a fail look like
A second destructive test described (nick-break or macro) and what it shows
Results recorded and compared with the specification before production

essays.stem: A trainee's 6 mm butt welds show (1) lack of root penetration, (2) porosity and (3) bad distortion. For each fault, give likely causes and explain how you would coach the trainee to put it right.
essays.modelAnswer: (1) Lack of root penetration is often caused by a root gap that is too small or a root face that is too thick, a nozzle that is too small, moving too fast, or the flame not pointed into the root. I would have him check the fit-up with a gauge, use the nozzle on the WPS, and watch for a small keyhole at the root as he welds. (2) Porosity can come from an oxidising flame, a dirty rod or plate, or lifting the flame away so the pool is left open to the air. I would show him how to set a true neutral flame, clean the joint and rod, and keep the outer flame over the pool, also at the end of the weld. (3) Distortion comes from too much heat, too few tacks and a poor welding order. I would show him how to tack closely, preset the plates, clamp or use chill bars, and weld in a planned order. Then I would watch him weld a test piece and check it with him.
markingPoints: Causes of lack of root penetration and how to correct them
Causes of porosity and how to correct them
Causes of distortion and how to correct them
Coaching approach: shows the method, then watches the trainee try and checks the result

essays.stem: Explain why gas welding thin sheet causes more distortion than arc welding the same sheet, and describe the methods you would use to control it.
essays.modelAnswer: A gas flame is less concentrated than an arc. It heats the metal more slowly and spreads the heat over a much wider area before the joint melts. A wide strip of the sheet expands, and when it cools and shrinks it pulls the sheet out of shape, so buckling and bending are worse than with an arc. To control it I would: keep the joint gap correct and tack at close, even spacing, starting in the middle and working out; set the gap a little wider at the far end of a long seam, because the gap closes as the weld moves along; preset parts so they pull back into line; clamp the work or use a jig; use copper or steel chill bars beside the seam to draw heat away; use the smallest nozzle that gives full fusion and weld at a steady speed; and use back-step or skip welding in short lengths so heat is not built up in one place. Small distortion left after welding may be corrected by planishing or flame straightening.
markingPoints: Explains the gas flame heats a wider area more slowly, so more expansion and shrinkage
Tacking, correct gap and tapered gap
Presetting, clamping, jigs and chill bars
Smallest suitable nozzle, steady speed, back-step or skip welding
Correction after welding (planishing or flame straightening)

essays.stem: Explain how gas welding a cast iron part differs from gas welding mild steel. Include the preparation, flux, filler rod, flame, preheat and cooling.
essays.modelAnswer: Cast iron is brittle and cracks easily if it is heated or cooled unevenly. Before welding, the crack or joint is cleaned of oil and dirt, and the ends of a crack may be drilled to stop it running. The edges are prepared with a V so the weld can reach the bottom. The whole part, or a wide area round the joint, is preheated slowly, often in a furnace or with a large flame, so it expands evenly. A cast iron filler rod is used with a cast iron flux, because the oxide on cast iron melts at a higher heat than the iron; mild steel needs no flux. The flame is neutral or very slightly carburising, never oxidising, which would burn the carbon. The welder keeps the pool fluid and works the flux in. After welding, the part is cooled very slowly, for example covered with dry sand or a heat blanket, so it does not crack or become hard. Mild steel is simpler: no preheat for thin parts, no flux, a neutral flame and normal cooling.
markingPoints: Cleaning, V preparation, and drilling crack ends
Slow, even preheat of the part
Cast iron rod and a flux are needed (mild steel needs no flux)
Neutral or slightly carburising flame, never oxidising
Very slow cooling to prevent cracking and hardness

essays.stem: You are in charge of a gas welding repair on a farm in St Elizabeth, away from the workshop. Explain how you would control the fire, gas, fume and burn hazards on site.
essays.modelAnswer: Before travelling I would check the gas set, the arrestors and hoses, and secure the cylinders upright on a trolley or in the vehicle, with valves shut and in a ventilated space. On site I would look at the work area: I would move dry grass, hay, fuel and anything that burns, or cover it with fire blankets, and wet the ground if it is very dry. I would check behind and under the work for fuel lines or tanks. I would place a fire extinguisher and water close by, and one person would act as fire watcher during the work and for some time after it. The cylinders would be kept upright, chained, in the shade, and away from the hot work. I would leak test the joints with soapy water after setting up. Everyone would wear goggles of the right shade, flame-resistant clothes, gloves and boots, and I would keep the farm workers back. If working in a shed, I would make sure there was good air flow for fumes. At the end I would shut down and bleed the set and check the area again before leaving.
markingPoints: Equipment checked and cylinders carried and secured upright with valves closed
Area cleared of things that burn; check behind and under the work
Extinguisher or water ready and a fire watch during and after
Leak test, cylinders kept upright, shaded and away from heat; ventilation for fumes
PPE, keeping others back, safe shut-down and final check of the area

essays.stem: Describe how to prepare, tack and gas weld a small-bore mild steel pipe butt joint in the fixed horizontal position (5G).
essays.modelAnswer: First I would cut the pipe ends square and bevel them if the wall is thick enough to need it, leaving a small root face. I would clean the ends inside and out, back to bright metal, and remove any burr. Then I would line the pipes up straight, using a clamp or angle iron, with an even root gap all round. I would place three or four small tacks evenly round the joint, check the alignment again and grind or blend the tack ends. With the pipe fixed, the weld is made in two halves. I would start just past the bottom (6 o'clock) and weld up one side over the top to just past 12 o'clock, then weld the other side from the bottom, overlapping the start and finish. I would keep a small pool, change the torch and rod angles as I go round, and watch for full penetration at the root, especially overhead at the bottom. After cooling I would inspect the outside and, if possible, the inside for penetration.
markingPoints: Cuts ends square, bevels if needed, and cleans inside and out
Lines up the pipes with an even gap; 3 or 4 even tacks
Welds in two halves from the bottom up over the top, overlapping starts and stops
Changes angles round the pipe and keeps a small pool with full penetration
Inspects the weld when cool

essays.stem: Explain how you would check an oxy-acetylene set for leaks and for faulty regulators and flashback arrestors, how you would take faulty parts out of use, and what you would report.
essays.modelAnswer: With the set assembled and the cylinder valves opened slowly, I would set the working pressures and close the torch valves. I would brush leak-test solution or soapy water on every joint, from the cylinder valves to the torch, and look for bubbles. Then I would close the cylinder valves and watch the gauges for a few minutes: if the high-pressure gauge falls, there is a leak; if the working gauge keeps rising with the torch shut, the regulator seat is letting by (creep). I would check the gauges read zero when empty and the glass is not cracked. The flashback arrestors would be checked for damage, date marks and any record of a flashback, and tested or replaced as the maker says. Any faulty part would be removed, tagged "Do not use" with the date and fault, and put in a locked quarantine place. I would report it in writing to the supervisor or the store, with the part, the fault, where it was used and who found it, and record the replacement.
markingPoints: Leak test with soapy water or leak-test solution on every joint
Gauge drop test for leaks and creep test for the regulator seat
Checks arrestors and gauges, tested or replaced as the maker says
Faulty part removed, tagged and kept away from use
Written report: part, fault, location, who found it, and the replacement

practical1.title: Rightward single-V butt welds in 6 mm plate to a group-written procedure, with bend tests and a test report
practical1.brief: Your group will plan, weld and test single-V butt joints in 6 mm mild steel plate using the rightward method. First, as a group, complete the WPS form the assessor gives: the joint preparation (about 60° V, root face and root gap), the nozzle size and gas pressures from the maker's chart, the flame type, the filler rod size and the welding order. One member leads the safety check of the gas sets (arrestors, hoses, leak test, cylinders secured) before any torch is lit. Every member then prepares, tacks and welds one butt joint (two plates about 150 mm × 75 mm) in the flat position, and writes their nozzle, pressures and weld time on the weld record. When the joints are cool, each member inspects another member's joint by eye and with a gauge, and records the face and root condition. The group then cuts two test strips from each of two joints chosen by the assessor, and bend tests them in a vice or press (one face bend and one root bend each). Write a short test report saying whether the procedure gave sound welds and what should change. Photograph each stage below. Hand in the WPS, the weld record, the inspection notes, the report and the photos once for the whole group.
materials: 6 mm mild steel plate, two pieces about 150 mm × 75 mm for each member, edges bevelled or ready to bevel
Copper-coated mild steel filler rod of the size given on the WPS
Oxy-acetylene sets on trolleys, with flashback arrestors, nozzle chart, spark lighter and tip cleaners
Leak-test solution or soapy water and a brush
Firebricks or a welding table, tongs, wire brushes, files and an angle grinder
Weld gauge, rule and a magnifier
Hacksaw or bandsaw, and a heavy vice or press with a former for bend tests
WPS form, weld record sheet and report sheet
photos: The gas sets checked and leak tested, with cylinders secured
A joint prepared and tacked, with the gap and V angle being measured
A neutral flame set, before welding
A finished weld, face side and root side
The bend test strips after testing
The weld record, inspection notes and test report
checklist: Helped complete the WPS and used the nozzle and pressures it gives
Set up, leak tested and lit the torch safely, and set a neutral flame
Prepared and tacked own joint with an even gap and correct V
Welded own joint by the rightward method with even penetration along the root
Inspected another member's weld accurately and recorded the faults found
Took part safely in the bend tests and recorded the result
Shut down and bled the set correctly and left the bay safe and tidy
safety: Check arrestors and hoses and leak test every joint before lighting; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Wear gas welding goggles of the right shade, flame-resistant clothing, leather gloves and boots
Keep cylinders upright and chained, and keep oil and grease away from oxygen fittings
Treat all metal as hot: use tongs and mark hot work
Wear eye protection and keep others clear when grinding, sawing and bend testing

practical2.title: Planned fabrication of a thin-sheet steel tray with distortion control, a leak test and a job record
practical2.brief: Your group will plan and make small open trays from 1.6 mm mild steel sheet, gas welded and then leak tested. The assessor gives a drawing of a tray about 200 mm × 150 mm × 50 mm. As a group, first write a short job plan: the cutting list, the joints (folded sides with welded corners, or separate pieces with corner and edge joints), the nozzle and pressures, the order of tacking and welding, and the steps you will take to control distortion (tack spacing, clamping, chill bars, welding order). Each member makes one tray: marks out, cuts and folds or fits the sheet, tacks it square, and gas welds the corners by the leftward method. One member leads the check of the gas sets before work starts, and another keeps the job record (gas used, time taken and problems). When the trays are cool, the group checks each one for size, squareness and flatness against the drawing and records the results. Then each tray is leak tested by filling it with water, or by the chalk and paraffin test, and any leaks are marked, re-welded and tested again. Photograph each stage below. Hand in the job plan, the check sheet, the job record and the photos once for the whole group.
materials: 1.6 mm mild steel sheet, enough for one tray per member as the cutting list gives
1.6 mm copper-coated mild steel filler rod
Oxy-acetylene sets with flashback arrestors, nozzle chart, spark lighter and tip cleaners
Snips or guillotine, and a folder (or separate pieces if no folder is available)
Clamps, a square, a rule, scriber and soapstone, and copper or steel chill bars
Firebricks, tongs, wire brushes and a file
Water, or chalk wash and paraffin, for the leak test; cloths and a drip tray
Drawing, job plan form, check sheet and job record sheet
photos: The job plan with the cutting list and welding order
Sheet marked out and cut, with the corners folded or fitted
A tray tacked and checked with a square
A corner being welded with clamps or chill bars in place
The finished trays, checked against the drawing
The leak test, with any leaks marked
The completed check sheet and job record
checklist: Took part in writing the job plan, including the distortion control steps
Marked out, cut and fitted own tray to the drawing
Tacked own tray square, with tacks evenly spaced
Welded the corners with full fusion and no burn-through
Own tray is within size and square, and sits flat
Carried out the leak test correctly and repaired any leak found
Recorded results honestly and left the bay safe and tidy
safety: Check and leak test the gas sets before lighting; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Wear gas welding goggles, flame-resistant clothing, leather gloves and boots
Handle cut sheet with gloves, as the edges are sharp; file off burrs
Keep paraffin away from the welding area and the flame; let trays cool before the leak test
Treat all metal as hot and mark hot work
